Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
List the indications for surgical hip dislocation in patients with a fracture.
Review the surgical anatomy and technique for surgical hip dislocation.
Discuss complications of surgical hip dislocation.
Introduction
Surgical hip dislocation represents a solution to the challenge of achieving safe surgical
exposures for the management of combined femoral head and acetabular fractures without
compromising femoral head blood supply.
Historically, surgical approaches for fractures of the femoral head and acetabulum were
varied. Posterior approaches were advocated by some because the posteriorly based blood
supply had already been traumatically disrupted.1

Anterior approaches allow for dislocation of the femoral head but afford limited access to the
posterior acetabulum.
A direct comparison of anterior and posterior approaches showed no difference with regard
osteonecrosis in the management of femoral head fractures.2

Introduction
Anatomic studies on femoral head perfusion served as the basis for additional advances
in developing surgical access to the femoral head and the acetabulum. The dominant
blood supply to the femoral head is posteriorly based, from lateral epiphyseal branches
of the medial femoral circumflex femoral artery.3-5 An understanding of the anatomic
basis of femoral head perfusion served as the foundation for surgical hip dislocation.3,6
Indications

Indications
Surgical hip dislocation is an option for the management of Pipkin type IV combined
femoral head and posterior wall acetabular fractures and also has been proposed for
use in isolated acetabular fractures. Injury features that may serve as specific indications
for surgical dislocation include acetabular fracture marginal impaction, comminuted
posterior wall fractures, intra-articular fragments, or considerable cranial extension of a
posterior wall fragment, including involvement of the superior acetabular rim.7
Combined femoral head and posterior-wall acetabulum fractures also warrant
consideration of surgical hip dislocation. Other indications include femoral head allograft
reconstruction (Figure 1). An analysis of femoral head fracture-dislocations showed a
high incidence of traumatic posterosuperior capsulolabral tears, an injury for which
surgical hip dislocation affords access for repair8

Figure 1 Images of the right hip of a 19-year-old man with hip pain and a femoral head

Management
Surgical Approach

Surgical Approach
To review an surgical approach see Video 1. The patient is placed in the lateral decubitus
position. The Kocher-Langenbeck, Gibson, or modified Gibson approach can be used
(Figure 2). In the Kocher-Langenbeck superficial dissection, the gluteus maximus fascia
and muscle are divided in line with their fibers. Subsequently, Gibson9 described a
slightly more anteriorly based limb of the cranial aspect of the incision and, rather than
dividing the gluteus maximus, reflected the entire gluteus maximus posteriorly. The
modified Gibson approach is a mid-lateral incision over the femur extending proximally,
longitudinally over the greater trochanter toward the iliac crest.10 The gluteal fascia is
then incised from the distal aspect to the greater trochanter and extended proximally.
The anterior border of the gluteus maximus is identified based on perforators from the
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004095

inferior gluteal artery. Additional retraction of the gluteus maximus is facilitated by
partial release of the gluteus maximus sling as it inserts broadly on the femur; however,
this is not usually necessary. The gluteus medius is retracted anteriorly with the use of a
curved Hohmann or cobra retractor placed in the interspinous notch.
Video 1 Shahien A, Kain MS, Tornetta P III, Wegrzyn K: Surgical Dislocation of the Hip for
Posterior Wall Fractures [video]. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, 2020.

Figure 2 Illustration shows superficial dissection for surgical hip dislocation. The Kocher-
Langenbeck incision (line A) splits the gluteus maximus in line with fibers above the
greater trochanter. The modified Gibson incision (line B) is a mid-lateral, longitudinal
incision. (Courtesy of L. Henry Goodnough, MD, Seattle, WA. Illustration by Sean Daley.)
A digastric trochanteric osteotomy is performed to facilitate deep exposure and hip
dislocation (Figure 3). First, the posterior border of the gluteus medius, along with its
tendinous insertion on the posterosuperior greater trochanter, is identified. Next, the
posterior border of the vastus origin is identified and mobilized from the vastus ridge. An
oscillating saw is used to initiate a step-cut osteotomy at the posterior border of the
greater trochanter. The step-cut should step down distally so that on reduction of the
osteotomy the pull of the abductor generates cranially directed compression of the step-
cut osteotomy. The osteotomy is completed with the use of osteotomes.

Figure 3 Illustrations of a hip show digastric osteotomy and surgical hip dislocation. A, A
step-cut, digastric osteotomy of the greater trochanter is performed. A Z-shaped
capsulotomy is performed before hip dislocation; this spares the posteryouiorly based
blood supply of the femoral head. B, Anterior dislocation of the femoral head. (Courtesy
of L. Henry Goodnough, MD, Seattle, WA. Illustration by Sean Daley.)
A Z-shaped capsulotomy is designed to spare the posterior-based blood supply to the
femoral head. The first limb is longitudinal (Figure 3) and is anterior to the lesser
trochanter to mitigate risk of damage to the medial femoral circumflex artery. The
second limb is vertical and anterolateral along the femoral neck, to the acetabulum,
short of the labrum. Then it curves posteriorly toward the piriformis. The hip is then
dislocated via flexion and external rotation. In the setting of trauma, oblique traumatic
tearing of the posterior capsule typically is observed. The traumatic capsulotomy must
be extended while preserving the posterior blood supply, and the hip can be dislocated
posteriorly.7
For visualization of the retro-acetabular surface, the piriformis and the obturator
externus tendons can be dissected, identified, and divided 1.5 cm from their insertion on
the proximal femur.
At the conclusion of the procedure, the trochanteric osteotomy is fixed with the use of
3.5-mm cortical screws.

Outcomes

Outcomes
In the initial description of surgical hip dislocation by Ganz et al,6 213 patients were
treated over a 7-year period. The main indications in this series were femoroacetabular
impingement, post-Perthes deformity, pigmented villonodular synovitis, synovial
chondromatosis,11 and cartilaginous exostosis. At minimum follow-up of 2 years, no
instances of osteonecrosis of the femoral head were reported.6 No surgical hip
dislocations in this initial series were performed after traumatic hip dislocation.
Subsequently, Siebenrock et al7 performed Ganz surgical hip dislocation (the Kocher-
Langenbeck approach with trochanteric flip osteotomy and surgical dislocation) in
patients with an acute fracture. Twelve patients with an acetabular fracture were
treated, with a minimum follow-up of 2 years. Eight patients underwent an anterior
dislocation, and four patients underwent a posterior dislocation, with the surgeons using
the traumatic capsular disruption present at injury. In this series, no instance of femoral
head osteonecrosis was reported.7
A prospective study of Pipkin type I and type II femoral head fractures managed via Ganz
surgical hip dislocation reported excellent patient-reported outcomes in 28 patients at a
minimum follow-up of 2 years. No instance of femoral head osteonecrosis was reported;
however, only Pipkin type I and type II fractures and patients treated via initial reduction
within 6 hours were included.8
Complications

Complications
Complications after surgical hip dislocation include osteonecrosis of the femoral head
(Figure 4), heterotopic ossification, and nonunion of the trochanteric osteotomy.
Although osteonecrosis is the dreaded complication after surgical hip dislocation,

contemporary studies have reported favorable results, with evidence of low rates of
osteonecrosis at a minimum follow-up of 2 years.6,7,12,13 Heterotopic ossification
occurred in four of the 12 patients in the series on surgical dislocation for fracture by
Ganz et al.7 Nonunion of trochanteric osteotomy is rare, and a step-cut morphology is
advocated to mitigate the risk of this complication.6
Figure 4 Radiographs of a left hip with osteonecrosis. A, Lateral radiograph
demonstrates the crescent sign (arrows). B, AP radiograph demonstrates mild flattening
of the femoral head (arrow). (Reproduced from Zalavras CG, Lieberman JR:
Osteonecrosis of the femoral head: Evaluation and treatment. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2014;22[7]:455-464.)
Pearls
Surgical dislocation is a safe option for the management of fractures of the acetabulum, the
femoral head, or combined injuries.
The surgical dislocation can be approached via the Kocher-Langenbeck or modified Gibson
intervals.

A step-cut digastric osteotomy of the greater trochanter allows for stable repair with low risk
of nonunion.
Rates of osteonecrosis, heterotopic ossification, and osteotomy nonunion are low after
surgical hip dislocation.
